title: Rehearse the end
hookLine: an old man's advice: rehearse death, so you can meet it well (Letters 26)
last: THE WATER CLOCK — NOTICE THE WATER RUNNING.

lines: SENECA IS OLD, AND SAYS SO.
cards: Actors rehearse the hardest scene the most. Pilots practice the engine failure in a simulator, over and over, so that on the real day their hands already know what to do. Nobody calls that morbid.
It's how you get calm about something you can't avoid. In the twenty-sixth letter, Seneca is old, and says so.
And he gives Lucilius a piece of advice borrowed, cheerfully, from a rival school, about the one scene everyone plays exactly once.

teach.h: AN OLD BODY, A YOUNG MIND.
teach.b: Seneca writes that his body is worn, but his mind feels young and glad to have less to do with the body. Old age, he says, has taken away his vices more than his strength.
He'll let death decide how far he has come. Talk is cheap; anyone can sound brave in a letter. The last day will show whether his calm was real or a performance.
So he prepares, the way a student prepares for an exam whose date is unknown. The advice comes from Epicurus, whose school disagreed with the Stoics about a great deal.
Seneca quotes him anyway: rehearse death. And he adds his own gloss: whoever tells you this is telling you to rehearse freedom. A person who has learned how to die has unlearned how to be a slave.
Fear of the end is the leash that lets everything else pull us around.
Look back at this week: a short walk and back to the mind, words that shape the soul, starting poor, deeds that match words, real joy, the water clock, and now this.

teach.h: THE WEEK: LIVE IT, NOT ONLY SAY IT.
teach.b: Every one asks the same thing: do you live it, or only say it?
Rehearsing the end asks it where it's hardest to fake.

how: Stoic practitioners sometimes keep a brief, calm reflection on their own mortality, often in the evening, and use it to set right something they would not want left undone.

o: a Latin prayer said at Roman funerals
dwell on death until you lose all hope
rehearse death, and so rehearse freedom

games.q: the old man's letter — tap the pairs.

s: Seneca refused to quote Epicurus because he belonged to a rival school
he quotes Epicurus often, including here: rehearse death.
Seneca says death will test how far he has really come
anyone can sound brave in a letter; the last day shows if the calm was real.
rehearsing death, for Seneca, is about being gloomy

games.q: you're old, and people praise your brave letters about death. how do you know your calm is real?
o: you'll let death be the examiner, and prepare until then.
games.why: Seneca says he'll let death judge his progress, so he rehearses: whoever has learned to die has unlearned slavery.

practice: This is gentle; if today is a hard day for it, simply rest with your breath instead. Otherwise, let one plain thought into the room, one day I'll end, without picturing how, and notice what your body does.
Then ask quietly what you'd want to have done, said or set right, and breathe with whatever answer comes.

wordCard.voice: Meditare mortem. Epicurus' advice, which Seneca borrows: rehearse death, because whoever has learned to die has unlearned slavery. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Seneca's rendering of Epicurus in Letters 26.8: rehearse (practice, think on) death.

carryVoice: Your line: ready, calmly. That's our week in Seneca's letters, start to finish. Next week, more letters.
